area.name: Kitchen and everyday life
area.blurb: Cook and store food safely, do laundry, and take the first big grown-up steps: renting, job hunting and voting.
area.intro: These guides cover skills you'll use almost every day once you live on your own. The kitchen guides follow U.S. food safety advice from USDA, FDA and CDC. The later guides cover renting, applying for a job and registering to vote, using U.S. rules that often differ from state to state.

guides.name: Use a Food Thermometer and Cook to Safe Temperatures
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help read the thermometer with an adult from about 8, and check food alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A food thermometer tells you when meat, poultry, egg dishes and leftovers are hot enough inside to be safe. You can't tell by looking. This guide gives the USDA safe minimum temperatures and shows you where to put the thermometer.
need: Food thermometer (a digital instant-read type is easiest to read)
Hot, soapy water to clean the thermometer
The safe temperature chart from FoodSafety.gov (the numbers are in step 1)
Oven mitts
before: Wash the thermometer stem in hot, soapy water before and after each use.
Read your thermometer's instructions so you know how deep to push it in. USDA says a digital instant-read thermometer needs to go in at least ½ inch, and a dial instant-read about 2 to 2½ inches.

steps.how: All poultry: 165 °F. Ground beef, pork, veal and lamb: 160 °F. Whole steaks, roasts and chops of beef, pork, veal and lamb: 145 °F, then a 3-minute rest. Fish: 145 °F. Egg dishes: 160 °F. Leftovers and casseroles: 165 °F.

steps.t: Check near the end of cooking
steps.how: Start checking a little before you expect the food to be done. USDA says it's safest to take the food off the heat before you take its temperature.
Push the tip into the thickest part of the food. Keep it from touching bone, fat or gristle.

steps.t: Go in from the side for thin foods
steps.how: For burgers and other thin foods, slide the thermometer in from the side until the tip reaches the center.

steps.t: Check whole birds in three places
steps.how: For a whole chicken or turkey, check the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing, and the thickest part of the breast. Every spot needs to reach 165 °F.

steps.t: Check mixed dishes in several spots
steps.how: For casseroles and egg dishes, check the center or thickest part, then a few other spots.
If any spot reads below the target, put the food back on the heat and check again later.
After steaks, chops and roasts reach 145 °F, let them sit 3 minutes before you cut or eat them. During the rest, the temperature holds steady or keeps rising, which finishes killing germs.
Wash the stem in hot, soapy water before you use it again.

how_it_works.subject: Biology
how_it_works.title: Why the inside temperature matters, and why color can fool you
body: Raw meat, poultry and eggs can carry harmful bacteria. Heat kills them, but only when the food gets hot enough all the way through. The outside of a chicken breast heats first and the center heats last. That's why you measure the thickest part.

Time matters too. After a steak or roast comes off the heat, its temperature stays the same or keeps rising for a few minutes, and that extra heat destroys bacteria. Because of this, USDA says whole cuts of pork cooked to 145 °F with a 3-minute rest are as safe as the old advice of 160 °F with no rest.

Color is a poor guide. Ground beef can turn brown inside before it's hot enough to kill bacteria. USDA reports that about 1 in 4 hamburgers turns brown in the middle before it reaches a safe temperature. A thermometer measures what matters: the temperature inside.
how_it_works.try: Make your own fridge chart. Write the safe temperatures in big numbers, sorted from highest to lowest, and draw where the thermometer goes in a chicken breast, a burger and a whole turkey. Then cover the numbers and quiz each other.

teach: Let your child read the number out loud while you hold the food steady.
Before the thermometer goes in, ask them to point to the thickest part.
Cut one cooked burger open together and talk about why you still check the temperature instead of trusting the color.
Give them the job of washing the thermometer after every use.
tips: Fish is done at 145 °F, or when the flesh is opaque and flakes easily with a fork.
Shrimp, lobster, crab and scallops are done when the flesh is pearly or white and opaque. Clams, oysters and mussels are done when the shells open.
Raw ham needs 145 °F and a 3-minute rest. Reheat precooked ham to 165 °F, or to 140 °F if it was packaged in a USDA-inspected plant.
Keep the thermometer in the same drawer every time so it's easy to grab.

mistakes.problem: Judging doneness by color.
mistakes.fix: Use the thermometer every time. Ground beef can look brown before it's safe.

mistakes.problem: The tip is touching bone.
mistakes.fix: Pull back a little and move the tip into the meat, away from bone, fat and gristle.

mistakes.problem: Checking only one spot in a whole bird or a casserole.
mistakes.fix: Check the thigh, wing and breast of a bird, or several spots in a casserole.

mistakes.problem: Using the thermometer on raw food, then cooked food, without washing it.
mistakes.fix: Wash the stem in hot, soapy water between uses.

mistakes.problem: Cutting into a roast the moment it comes out.
mistakes.fix: Let whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal rest 3 minutes after they reach 145 °F.

safety: Use a food thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes and leftovers. Color and texture aren't reliable signs of safety.
Take food off the heat before you take its temperature.
Wash the thermometer in hot, soapy water before and after each use.

guides.name: Store Leftovers Safely
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help pack leftovers from about 7, and put food away alone from about 10.
guides.intro: Leftovers save money and time, but they need to get cold fast. Bacteria multiply quickly in food left at room temperature. These steps follow USDA advice for cooling, storing and reheating leftovers.
need: Shallow containers with lids
Tape or labels and a marker
Appliance thermometer for the fridge and freezer
Food thermometer for reheating
before: Use an appliance thermometer to check that your fridge is at 40 °F or below and your freezer is at 0 °F or below.

steps.how: Get leftovers into the fridge within 2 hours after cooking. If it's hotter than 90 °F, like at a summer picnic, the limit is 1 hour.
Divide large amounts into shallow containers so the food cools quickly.
You don't have to wait for food to cool on the counter. Hot food can go straight into the fridge, or you can chill it first in a bowl of ice or cold water.
Write what it is and the date on the lid so you know when to use it.

steps.t: Eat or freeze within 3 to 4 days
steps.how: Leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge. If you won't eat them by then, freeze them.
Frozen food stays safe, but leftovers taste best if you eat them within 3 to 4 months.
Thaw frozen leftovers in the fridge, in cold water in a leak-proof bag, or in the microwave. Never thaw on the counter. You can also reheat straight from frozen; it just takes longer.
Heat leftovers until a food thermometer reads 165 °F. Bring sauces, soups and gravy to a rolling boil.
Cover the food and stir or turn it while it heats. Let it stand for a bit, then check the temperature in several places.

steps.t: Toss food left out too long
steps.how: Throw away perishable food that sat out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90 °F). Reheating won't fix it, because some bacteria make toxins that cooking doesn't destroy.

how_it_works.subject: Biology
how_it_works.title: The danger zone and doubling bacteria
body: Bacteria grow fastest between 40 °F and 140 °F. Food safety experts call this the danger zone. In that range, the number of bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes.

Doubling adds up fast. Start with 10 bacteria. After 20 minutes there could be 20, then 40, then 80. Two hours holds six 20-minute doublings, so 10 could become 10 × 2⁶ = 640. That's why the 2-hour rule exists.

Cold slows bacteria down, and freezing makes them go dormant, like they're asleep. Freezing doesn't kill them. When food thaws, they wake up and can multiply again. Some bacteria also make toxins that heat can't destroy, so reheating can't rescue food that sat out too long.

Shallow containers help because heat escapes through the food's surface. A thin, wide layer has lots of surface for its size, so its middle cools fast. A deep pot keeps its center warm for a long time.
how_it_works.formula: bacteria = starting number × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of 20-minute doublings
how_it_works.try: Make a doubling chart on paper. Put 1 dried bean in the first square. Each new square gets double the beans of the one before. Stop after 6 doublings, which is 2 hours in the danger zone. How many beans are in the last square?

teach: Set a 2-hour timer when food comes off the stove and put your child in charge of it.
Let them pick the containers and write the labels.
Show them the fridge thermometer and have them check it once a week.
tips: Small portions cool faster and are easier to reheat.
Cooked rice that sits out too long is a common cause of one type of food poisoning, so get it into a shallow container and into the fridge quickly.
Takeout and restaurant leftovers follow the same 2-hour rule.
Freezing keeps food safe, but it doesn't kill germs. Treat thawed food like fresh perishable food.

mistakes.problem: Leaving a big pot of soup on the stove to cool overnight.
mistakes.fix: Split it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

mistakes.problem: Reheating only until it's warm.
mistakes.fix: Heat to 165 °F and check in several spots.

mistakes.problem: Thawing leftovers on the counter.
mistakes.fix: Thaw in the fridge, in cold water in a sealed bag, or in the microwave.

mistakes.problem: Keeping leftovers for a week or more.
mistakes.fix: Eat them within 3 to 4 days, or freeze them.

mistakes.problem: Not knowing how cold the fridge is.
mistakes.fix: Keep an appliance thermometer inside and make sure it reads 40 °F or below.

safety: Refrigerate perishable food within 2 hours, or within 1 hour if it's above 90 °F.
Keep the fridge at 40 °F or below and the freezer at 0 °F or below.
Reheat leftovers to 165 °F. Bring sauces, soups and gravy to a rolling boil.

sources.name: USDA FSIS: Leftovers and Food Safety
USDA FSIS: How Temperatures Affect Food
FoodSafety.gov: 4 Steps to Food Safety
CDC: Preventing Food Poisoning

guides.name: Basic Knife Skills
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, cut with an adult right beside you from about 8, and use a chef's knife alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A sharp knife and a few good habits make cutting faster and safer. This guide covers how to hold the knife, how to hold the food, and how to wash and put knives away.
need: Chef's knife (8 to 10 inches), which handles most cutting jobs
Paring knife (3 to 4 inches) for small jobs
Cutting board
Damp kitchen towel, or a board with rubber feet
Practice foods like a zucchini, cucumber or potato
before: Put a damp towel under the cutting board, or use a board with rubber feet, so it can't slide.
Always cut on a cutting board. Never cut food while holding it in your hand.

steps.how: Set the board on a damp kitchen towel so it stays put while you cut.
Hold the handle close to the blade. This gives you better control.
With your other hand, hold the food with your fingertips curled under, like a claw. Tuck your thumb and little finger behind your other fingers, so your knuckles face the blade.
Round foods roll. Cut a potato or onion in half first, then set it flat side down before you keep cutting.

steps.t: Keep the tip on the board
steps.how: Cut with a rocking or see-saw motion, pushing slightly forward and away from your body. Keep the tip of the knife touching the board.
Let the sharp edge do the work. Smooth strokes beat hard pressing.
If a knife slips off the counter, step back and let it drop. Never try to catch it.
Carry a knife with the blade pointed down. Hand it over handle first, or set it down so the other person can pick it up.
Wash knives by hand after each use and dry them. Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water, where someone could reach in and get cut.
Store knives in a knife block, on a magnetic strip, or with a blade guard. If you pause while cutting, lay the knife at the top of the board with the blade facing away from you.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why a sharp knife cuts with less force
body: Pressure is how much force pushes on each bit of area. The formula is pressure = force ÷ area. Push with the same force on a smaller area, and the pressure goes up.

A sharp knife's edge is very thin, so it touches the food along a tiny area. A small push makes a big pressure, and the food splits apart. A dull edge is wider and rounder. The same push spreads out, so the knife squashes or slides instead of cutting.

Here's an example with made-up numbers. A 5-pound push on an edge touching 0.01 square inch makes 5 ÷ 0.01 = 500 pounds per square inch (psi). The same push on a duller edge touching 0.1 square inch makes only 50 psi.
That's why a sharp knife is safer. A dull knife needs more force, and extra force makes it easier for the blade to slip off the food.
how_it_works.try: Press a wooden craft stick into a lump of modeling clay two ways, using the same gentle push: first flat side down, then thin edge down. The edge sinks much deeper because the same force is squeezed onto a smaller area.

teach: Practice the claw with no knife at all. Curl your fingers on a zucchini and 'walk' them back.
Start with a steady food, like a zucchini cut in half and set flat side down, and stay right beside your child.
Teach 'step back, don't catch' before the very first lesson.
Have them say the habit out loud: 'Board steady, claw hand, tip down.'
tips: A serrated knife works well for bread and soft produce.
Keep knives sharp with a sharpening steel or a pull-through sharpener. Don't try to sharpen serrated knives at home.
Hold a few knives in your hand before you buy one, and pick the handle that feels comfortable.
Keep knives out of the dishwasher. Wash and dry them by hand.

mistakes.problem: Cutting food while holding it in the air.
mistakes.fix: Always set the food on the cutting board first.

mistakes.problem: Fingers flat on top of the food.
mistakes.fix: Curl them into a claw with your thumb tucked behind.

mistakes.problem: The board slides around.
mistakes.fix: Put a damp towel or a rubber-footed board underneath.

mistakes.problem: Round food rolls away.
mistakes.fix: Cut a flat side first and set it down on that side.

mistakes.problem: Pressing hard with a dull knife.
mistakes.fix: Sharpen it. A sharp knife needs less force and is less likely to slip.

safety: Use a cutting board, never your hand.
Never try to catch a falling knife.
Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water.
Carry knives blade down and pass them handle first.

guides.name: Cook Three Staples: Rice, Eggs and Pasta
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help at the stove from about 9, and cook these alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Rice, eggs and pasta are cheap, filling and the start of many meals. Learn these three and you can always make dinner. Each one also shows a bit of kitchen chemistry.
need: 2- to 3-quart saucepan with a tight-fitting lid (rice)
Large pot that holds more than 4 quarts of water (pasta)
Colander
Frying pan, bowl, fork and spatula (eggs)
Measuring cups
Oven mitts
before: Wash your hands before you start.
Read the package directions for your rice and pasta. Different kinds need different amounts of water and time.

steps.how: Put 1 cup of long-grain white rice and 1¾ to 2 cups of water in a 2- to 3-quart saucepan.
Bring it to a boil, stirring once or twice. Turn the heat down low, cover with a tight lid, and simmer 15 minutes. Brown rice needs 2 to 2½ cups of water and 45 to 50 minutes.
If the rice isn't tender or there's still water, cover and cook 2 to 4 minutes more. Take it off the heat, fluff it with a fork, cover, and let it stand 5 minutes.
Use about 4 quarts of water for each pound of pasta. Keep the lid on so it boils sooner.
Add the pasta to the boiling water and stir. Stir again once it starts cooking so the pieces don't stick together.
Cook for the time on the package. Taste a piece; it should be a little chewy. Pour it into a colander in the sink, keeping your face away from the steam.
Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork until blended.
Heat a frying pan with a little butter or oil over medium heat. Pour in the eggs and stir gently as they set. Keep cooking until no runny egg is left; scrambled eggs should not be runny.
Wash anything raw egg touched with hot, soapy water. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Hard-cooked eggs keep up to 1 week in the fridge.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: Starch soaks up water, and egg proteins unfold and set
body: Rice and pasta are mostly starch, packed into tiny grains called granules. When starch is heated in water, the granules soak up water and swell. Food scientists call this gelatinization. It's why hard rice turns soft, and why 1 cup of dry rice makes about 3 cups cooked.
Gelatinization only goes one way. Once the granules have swelled, cooked rice can't turn back into hard, raw grains.

Eggs change in a different way. Egg white is full of proteins. Each protein is a long chain folded into a special shape. Heat breaks the weak bonds holding that shape, so the proteins unfold. This is called denaturing. The unfolded proteins take up more room and tangle together, so a clear, runny egg white turns white and firm.
Cooking eggs until both white and yolk are firm also matters for safety. USDA notes that even clean, uncracked eggs can carry Salmonella bacteria.
how_it_works.formula: 1 cup dry rice + about 2 cups water → about 3 cups cooked rice
how_it_works.try: With an adult, measure ¼ cup of dry rice, cook it, and measure it again when it's done. How many times bigger did it get? The extra volume is water the starch soaked up.

teach: Let your child measure the rice and water. It's good practice with fractions.
Have them set a kitchen timer for each step.
Stand beside them the first few times they drain pasta, and show how to pour away from their face.
Have them crack eggs into a small bowl first, so any bits of shell are easy to scoop out.
tips: Keep the lid on while rice simmers so the steam stays in.
Instant rice and flavored rice mixes have their own directions; follow the package.
Cook egg casseroles and quiche to 160 °F, checked with a food thermometer.
Don't wash eggs before storing them. Keep them in their carton in the fridge, not in the door.

mistakes.problem: Lifting the lid again and again while rice cooks.
mistakes.fix: Keep it covered for the full time, then check.

mistakes.problem: Pasta clumps together.
mistakes.fix: Use about 4 quarts of water per pound, and stir right after adding it and again once it starts cooking.

mistakes.problem: Runny scrambled eggs.
mistakes.fix: Keep cooking until no liquid egg is left and they're firm.

mistakes.problem: Leaving the pot of rice on the stove all afternoon.
mistakes.fix: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours in a shallow container.

safety: Cook eggs until both the white and yolk are firm.
Cook casseroles and other egg dishes to 160 °F.
Wash utensils and counters that touched raw egg with hot, soapy water.
Drain pasta carefully and keep your face away from the steam.

guides.name: Do a Load of Laundry
guides.time: about 15 minutes of hands-on work, plus machine time
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help sort and load from about 7, and do a load alone from about 10.
guides.intro: Clean clothes start with the care label. Then you sort, pick a water temperature, measure detergent and let the machines work. One small habit, cleaning the dryer's lint filter, also lowers the risk of a dryer fire.
need: Laundry detergent
The detergent's measuring cap or a measuring cup
Washer and dryer, or a drying rack
Your machines' owner's manuals
before: Make sure the lint filter is in the dryer. Never run a dryer without it.
Check that the washer and dryer are plugged directly into wall outlets.

steps.how: U.S. clothing labels must tell you how to wash and dry the item and warn you about steps that would harm it. If a label lists a water temperature, don't go hotter. Follow any 'Do not bleach' or 'Dry flat' instructions.
Keep whites away from colors. Wash very dirty clothes apart from lightly dirty ones, lint-shedding items apart from others, and delicate items apart from sturdy ones.
Some colored clothes bleed dye. If an item's color runs, wash it alone or with clothes of the same color.
Rub a little liquid detergent into collars, cuffs and other heavily soiled spots before washing.

Follow the label first. Hot water cleans heavy dirt and kills more germs, but it can fade some colors. Warm water handles lightly soiled clothes and is safe for most colors. Cold water suits some delicate fabrics; use a detergent made for cold water.
Use the amount on the detergent package for your load size and how dirty it is. Too much makes extra suds that keep clothes from getting clean. Too little leaves dirt and body oil behind.
Don't stuff the washer. Clothes need room to move so water and detergent can flow through them. If your washer has a water-level setting, match it to the load.
Before and after every dryer load, pull out the lint filter and clear off the lint.
Tumble dry, hang or lay flat, whichever the label says. Check for stains before anything goes in the dryer; see the stain guide.

pro: Have your dryer installed and serviced by a professional, as the U.S. Fire Administration recommends.
If the outdoor vent flap doesn't open while the dryer runs, or the vent behind the dryer is crushed or blocked, get it fixed before you use the dryer again.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: How detergent pulls grease off clothes
body: Water alone can't wash away grease, because oil and water don't mix. Detergent fixes that. Its molecules have two ends. One end is attracted to water (hydrophilic, 'water-loving'). The other end is attracted to oil (hydrophobic, 'water-fearing').

In the wash, the oil-loving ends grab onto grease and body oil. The detergent molecules gather into tiny balls called micelles, with the oil trapped inside and the water-loving ends facing out. Now the water can carry the oil away when the washer drains and rinses.
Detergent also holds loosened dirt in the wash water so it doesn't settle back onto your clothes. That only works if the water can move, which is one reason not to overload the washer.
how_it_works.try: Pour water into a clear jar and add a spoonful of cooking oil. Put the lid on, shake, and watch the oil float back to the top. Now add a drop of dish soap, shake again, and look: the oil breaks into tiny drops that stay mixed in the water.

teach: Make sorting a game with three piles: whites, darks, and 'ask me.'
Read care labels together and match them to the machine settings.
Make cleaning the lint filter your child's job every single time.
Let them measure detergent with the cap and find the fill line.
tips: Mix small items with large ones, like washcloths with sheets, so everything moves freely.
Care labels may use symbols instead of words. In the U.S., the FTC allows the ASTM symbol system.
A label that says 'Only non-chlorine bleach, when needed' means chlorine bleach would harm the item.
Check clothes as they come out of the dryer. If you see a spot, rub in a little detergent and wash again.

mistakes.problem: Washing a new red shirt with whites.
mistakes.fix: Keep whites apart, and wash new colors alone or with similar colors.

mistakes.problem: Adding extra detergent 'to be safe.'
mistakes.fix: Measure what the package says. Too many suds keep clothes from getting clean.

mistakes.problem: Stuffing the washer full.
mistakes.fix: Leave room for clothes to move.

mistakes.problem: Skipping the lint filter.
mistakes.fix: Clean it before and after every load.

mistakes.problem: Ignoring the care label.
mistakes.fix: Check it first, especially for 'Dry flat', 'Do not bleach' and temperature limits.

safety: Clean the lint filter before and after each dryer cycle.
Never run the dryer without the lint filter.
Plug washers and dryers directly into wall outlets.
Clean the dryer vent ductwork every year.

guides.name: Remove Common Stains
guides.time: about 15 minutes, plus soaking and washing
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help blot and rinse from about 8, and treat everyday stains alone from about 12. Handle anything with bleach together with an adult.
guides.intro: Most stains come out if you act quickly and use the right method. The trick is knowing what kind of stain you have. This guide covers the basic rules and a few common stains.
need: Clean white cloths or paper towels for blotting
Liquid laundry detergent
Enzyme pretreatment or presoak product
A bowl or sink of cold water
Rubber gloves if you use bleach
before: Read the care label and the stain remover's label before you start.
Test any stain remover on a hidden spot, like a hem or seam allowance, to make sure it doesn't change the color.
When you use bleach or other strong products, open windows or work in a spot with plenty of fresh air.

steps.how: Treat stains as soon as you can. Fresh stains come out much more easily than old ones.
Press a clean cloth on a wet spill to soak it up. Rubbing can spread the stain and damage the fibers. Work from the back of the fabric to push the stain out.
Protein stains include blood, egg and grass. Oily stains include grease and cooking oil. Some, like chocolate, are both.

Soak blood, egg or grass stains in cold water; hot water can set them. For dried stains, scrape off what you can, then soak in cold water with detergent or an enzyme presoak. Don't use enzyme presoaks on silk or wool.
Rub full-strength liquid laundry detergent into the grease. Then wash in the hottest water the care label allows.
If some color remains, an all-fabric (oxygen) bleach is the gentler choice. Use chlorine bleach only if the fabric can take it, and never on silk, wool or spandex.
Rinse out the stain remover, then wash the item following its care label.
Look closely before anything goes in the dryer. Dryer heat can make a stain permanent. If it's still there, treat it and wash again, or let it air dry.

pro: For 'Dryclean only' clothes, take the stain to a dry cleaner. Home dry-cleaning solvents can be highly toxic.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: Three ways to break up a stain
body: Stain removers work in three main ways. Enzymes are proteins that break big molecules into small pieces. Enzyme pretreatments break down protein stains like blood and grass so water can wash them away.
Detergents and solvents go after oily stains. Oil doesn't mix with water, so you need something that grabs onto oil, like the detergent molecules in the laundry guide.

Bleach is an oxidizer. Color comes from parts of molecules called chromophores. Bleach breaks chemical bonds in those parts, so the molecule stops absorbing visible light and the color disappears. That's why bleach can lift a stain, and also why it can fade your shirt.
Heat matters too. Hot water can set protein stains, a bit like the way heat sets an egg white. That's why blood goes in cold water.
how_it_works.try: Rub a little grass onto two scraps of old white cotton. Rinse one in cold water right away. Leave the other for a day. Then wash both the same way and compare. Which one came cleaner?

teach: Keep a small stain kit (cloths, liquid detergent, enzyme pretreatment) where kids can reach it.
Teach the short rule: blot, cold water, check before drying.
Store bleach and other cleaners up high and out of sight of young children, and use bleach together until your child is older.
tips: If you can't tell what a stain is, skip hot water.
For chocolate, rub in liquid detergent first for the oily part, then treat any color that's left.
Rinse stain remover out before washing so it can't react with other products.
Never iron a stained spot. Heat sets stains.

mistakes.problem: Scrubbing hard at a fresh spill.
mistakes.fix: Blot gently, working from the back of the fabric.

mistakes.problem: Rinsing blood in hot water.
mistakes.fix: Use cold water. Heat sets protein stains.

mistakes.problem: Drying a shirt before the stain is gone.
mistakes.fix: Check first. Treat and rewash if needed.

mistakes.problem: Using chlorine bleach on wool, silk or spandex.
mistakes.fix: Check the label and use only what it allows.

mistakes.problem: Mixing cleaners to make them 'stronger.'
mistakes.fix: Never mix bleach with ammonia, acids like vinegar, or any other cleaner.

safety: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner. Bleach plus ammonia makes chloramine gas. Bleach plus acids, including vinegar and some toilet bowl cleaners, makes chlorine gas.
Read and follow the safety instructions on every product you use.
Wear gloves and keep fresh air flowing when you use bleach.
Store bleach up, away and out of sight of children.

guides.name: Rent Your First Place
guides.time: a few weeks of planning before you move
guides.teach_age: Talk through a rent budget together from about 12, compare real listings from about 15, and sign a lease yourself once you're an adult.
guides.intro: Renting your first apartment is a big money step and a legal one. A lease is a contract, so you need to know what you're signing. This guide covers budgeting, spotting scams, reading the lease, deposits, renters insurance and the move-in check. Tenant laws are different in each state, so always check your own state's rules.
need: Your monthly income and a simple budget
Money for move-in costs, such as the first month's rent and a security deposit
A phone camera
A notebook or move-in checklist
A folder for your lease, receipts and photos
before: Look up your state's tenant rights before you sign anything. USA.gov points to state housing agencies, attorneys general and state tenant handbooks.

steps.how: HUD counts a household as 'cost burdened' when housing costs, including utilities, are more than 30% of its monthly income. Aim to keep rent plus utilities at or under that line.
Ask which utilities you'll pay, such as electricity, gas, water, trash and internet. Get the answer in writing.

See the place in person if you can. Search the address along with the owner's or company's name to check for copied listings. Walk away if someone rushes you or wants payment by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency.
Read every line before you sign, and ask about anything you don't understand. Don't count on promises that aren't written in the lease. Keep a signed copy.

A security deposit is money the landlord holds in case of unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. State law sets the limits. In Massachusetts, for example, the deposit can't be more than the first month's rent.

Your landlord's insurance covers the building, not your belongings. Renters insurance can pay to repair or replace your things if they're damaged or stolen, and its liability part helps if you're blamed for someone's injury or property damage.

On move-in day, walk through every room. Write down every problem and take photos. If your state uses a move-in 'statement of condition' form, fill it out. This keeps you from being blamed for damage you didn't cause.
Pay rent on time and get a receipt every time you pay. Massachusetts, for example, gives tenants the right to a receipt for every payment.
Report problems to your landlord in writing; email counts. Keep copies of what you send and what you get back.
If you have a dispute, reread your lease first. Then contact your state's tenant rights agency, your attorney general's office, or legal aid.

pro: If you can't settle a problem with your landlord, look for free or low-cost legal aid, or contact your state attorney general or housing agency.

how_it_works.subject: Economics
how_it_works.title: The 30 percent line, and why a lease is a contract
body: Rent is usually the biggest bill a renter pays each month. HUD uses 30% of income as a common line. When housing costs, including utilities, take more than 30% of a household's monthly income, HUD calls that household cost burdened. Less money is left for food, transportation and savings.

You can turn the line into a quick check: multiply your monthly income by 0.30. With a made-up monthly income of $2,000, that's 0.30 × 2,000 = $600 for rent plus utilities. If a place costs more, you'd need more income, a roommate or a cheaper place.

Renting has a civics side too. A lease is a contract, a set of promises the law will enforce. Most rules about deposits, repairs and evictions come from state and local law, which is why they vary so much. For example, the Massachusetts Attorney General says a landlord there can never force a tenant to move out without going to court first.
how_it_works.formula: most you'd spend on housing ≈ 0.30 × monthly income (rent + utilities)
how_it_works.try: Pick a real apartment listing near you. Add the rent and your best guess for utilities. Then work backward: divide that total by 0.30 to find the monthly income you'd need to stay at or under 30%.

teach: Look at real rental listings together and add up the full monthly cost.
Read a sample lease out loud and circle anything confusing.
Practice a move-in walk-through in your own home: list every scuff and take photos.
Talk about scams. What would make a deal seem too good to be true?
tips: Rent that's much cheaper than similar places nearby can be a sign of a scam.
Get every promise in writing. Email counts.
Keep your lease, receipts, photos and repair emails together in one folder.
Ask whether a renters policy pays replacement cost (new items) or actual cash value (what your used items were worth). Replacement cost costs more but pays more.

mistakes.problem: Budgeting for rent but forgetting utilities.
mistakes.fix: Ask which utilities you pay and add them to the total.

mistakes.problem: Paying a deposit for a place you haven't checked out.
mistakes.fix: Visit if you can, search the address and owner, and never pay by wire, gift card or crypto.

mistakes.problem: Signing a lease you only skimmed.
mistakes.fix: Read every line and get any promises written in.

mistakes.problem: Skipping the move-in check.
mistakes.fix: List every problem and take photos on day one.

mistakes.problem: Assuming the landlord's insurance covers your stuff.
mistakes.fix: It doesn't. Get renters insurance.

safety: Never pay rent or a deposit by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency. The FTC says anyone who insists on those is running a scam.

guides.name: Apply for a Job
guides.time: a few hours over a week or two
guides.teach_age: Practice a résumé and a mock interview from about 13, and apply for a first job from about 14 to 16, depending on federal and state rules.
guides.intro: A first job teaches skills you can't learn in class and gives you money you earned yourself. Getting hired takes a few pieces: a résumé, references, a careful application, a good interview and a thank-you note. If you're under 18, federal and state laws limit when and where you can work.
need: Your phone number and a professional email address
A list of your school, activities, and any work or volunteer experience with dates
Two to three references who've agreed to be contacted
Printed copies of your résumé
A work permit or age certificate, if your state requires one
before: If you're under 18, check your state labor department's rules. Federal law doesn't require work permits, but many states do for workers of certain ages.

steps.t: Check the rules for your age
steps.how: Under federal law, 16 is the basic minimum age for most jobs. At 14 and 15 you can work only certain non-hazardous jobs, outside school hours: no more than 3 hours on a school day and 18 hours in a school week. If state and federal rules differ, the stricter one applies.
Write down your contact details, your school, your activities, and any jobs or volunteer work with dates and contact names.

List your education, any work or volunteer experience, activities, awards and skills. Start each bullet with an action verb. Keep it to one page in 10- to 12-point type, and ask someone to proofread it.
Pick teachers, school leaders, past employers or other adults who know your work, not family or friends. Ask them first, and tell them they may get a call.

steps.t: Write a short cover letter if asked
steps.how: Say which job you want and why you're interested in that business. Then connect your skills to the most important things the job needs.
Answer every question, and write 'N/A' instead of leaving a blank. On paper, use black or blue ink, spell carefully, and sign and date it. Proofread before you turn it in.
Learn the basics about the business. Practice answers to common interview questions out loud, and write down a few questions to ask them.
Dress for the job, silence your phone and arrive 15 minutes early. Bring copies of your résumé, a separate list of two to three references, your questions, and a notebook and pen.
Within a day, send each interviewer a short thank-you note or email.
If you haven't heard back within a week, call the person who set up your interview.

pro: If an employer asks you to work hours or do tasks that seem off-limits for your age, contact your state labor department or the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division.

how_it_works.subject: Economics
how_it_works.title: Trading your time and skills for pay
body: A job is a trade. You give an employer your time and skills, and the employer pays you wages. Businesses hire when they have work that needs doing and believe you can do it well.

Employers can't see your skills just by looking at you. A résumé, references and an interview are how you show them. A careful application and a thank-you note are evidence that you're reliable, which is part of what they're paying for.

Your pay depends on your wage and your hours. Gross pay, your pay before anything is taken out, equals hourly wage × hours worked. If you're 14 or 15, federal law caps a school week at 18 hours and a non-school week at 40 hours, so those limits shape how much you can earn.
how_it_works.formula: gross pay = hourly wage × hours worked
how_it_works.try: Find a real job posting near you that lists an hourly wage. Work out the gross pay for an 18-hour school week and a 40-hour summer week.

teach: Hold a mock interview at the kitchen table, then trade roles.
Help your child list everything they've done: babysitting, volunteering, clubs, sports, yard work for neighbors.
Proofread the résumé together, out loud.
Practice thank-you notes on something easy first, like a note to a relative for a gift.
tips: Use a simple, professional email address. Avoid nicknames.
Keep your voicemail greeting professional and check messages often while you're job hunting.
Make sure the dates and details on your résumé match your application.

For 14- and 15-year-olds, federal law allows work only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., except June 1 through Labor Day, when the evening limit is 9 p.m. Federal law doesn't limit hours for 16- and 17-year-olds in non-hazardous jobs, but many states do.

mistakes.problem: Listing references without asking them.
mistakes.fix: Ask first, and let them know a call may come.

mistakes.problem: Leaving blanks on the application.
mistakes.fix: Answer every question. Write 'N/A' if it doesn't apply.

mistakes.problem: Sending the same letter everywhere.
mistakes.fix: Name the job and the business, and match your skills to what they need.

mistakes.problem: Arriving right on time, or late.
mistakes.fix: Plan your route and arrive 15 minutes early.

mistakes.problem: Never following up.
mistakes.fix: Send a thank-you within a day, and call if you've heard nothing in a week.

guides.name: Register to Vote and Get Ready to Vote
guides.time: about 15 minutes to register, plus time to learn your ballot
guides.teach_age: Talk about elections from about 8, read a sample ballot together from about 12, and register yourself when your state allows, which in most states can be before you turn 18.
guides.intro: Voting is how citizens choose the people who make laws and run government. Before you can vote, most states require you to register, and each state sets its own deadlines and rules. This guide walks through the steps. It doesn't tell you who or what to vote for.
need: Your state or local election office's website (vote.gov links to every state)
Your home address
An ID, if your state requires one to vote
A calendar for deadlines

steps.how: To vote, you must be a U.S. citizen, meet your state's residency rules, be 18 by Election Day, and be registered by your state's deadline. North Dakota doesn't require voter registration.
There's no national registration deadline. Some states close registration 30 days before Election Day, and others let you register on Election Day itself.

Most states let you register online. You can also mail in the National Mail Voter Registration Form (New Hampshire, North Dakota, Wisconsin and Wyoming don't accept it), or register in person at your election office or state motor vehicles office.
In most states you can sign up before you turn 18. Several states let 17-year-olds vote in primary elections if they'll be 18 by the general election.

Look yourself up on your state's election website. Make sure your name, address and polling place are right. Check before the registration deadline so there's time to fix problems, and update it if you've moved.
Many election offices post sample ballots online. Read about each race and any ballot questions. If you use a voter guide, check who wrote it.

Most people who vote on Election Day vote in person at an assigned location. Some states hold elections entirely by mail, and others let you request an absentee ballot. Ask your election office which options you have.
Voting hours and locations are set locally. Confirm your voting location and its hours with your election office before each election.
Check your state's ID rules. In most states you need ID to vote in person. You don't need a voter registration card.

pro: If you have questions about whether you can vote or about your registration, contact your state or local election office.

how_it_works.subject: Civics
how_it_works.title: How your vote turns into representation
body: The United States is a representative democracy. Instead of voting on every law, citizens elect people to make laws for them. You vote for leaders at every level: local, state and federal.
In Congress, the House of Representatives has 435 members, and each serves a two-year term. The Senate has 100 senators, two from each state, and each serves a six-year term.

All 435 House seats are on the ballot every two years. Senate terms are staggered, so only about one-third of senators are elected in any two-year cycle. Midterm elections fall halfway between presidential elections.
how_it_works.try: Look up who represents you in Congress and when your state's next election is. Make a family calendar with the registration deadline circled in red.

teach: Read a sample ballot together and look up what each office does.
Practice finding your state's election office website.
Teach the process, not the choices. Let kids form their own views as they grow.
Mark registration deadlines and election dates on the family calendar.
tips: Register early instead of waiting for deadline week.
Check your registration again after any move.
Mail ballots can go back by mail, to your local election office, or in an official drop box, which needs no stamp.
If your registration shows as 'inactive,' contact your election office early. You may need extra steps before you can vote.

mistakes.problem: Missing the registration deadline.
mistakes.fix: Look up your state's deadline early. Some states close registration 30 days before Election Day.

mistakes.problem: Assuming you're still registered after a move.
mistakes.fix: Check your registration and update your address.

mistakes.problem: Going to the wrong voting location.
mistakes.fix: Confirm your location and hours with your election office before Election Day.

mistakes.problem: Seeing the ballot for the first time in the booth.
mistakes.fix: Read your sample ballot ahead of time.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting ID.
mistakes.fix: Check your state's ID rules before you go.
